Issued at 313 PM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

Early Wednesday afternoon, temperatures were in the mid to upper 60s 
and skies were mostly clear over central Kentucky and southern 
Indiana. A 1008mb surface low was located over east-central 
Illinois, with a cold front extending southward through southern 
Illinois and southeast Missouri. Elevated showers and thunderstorms, 
which generated severe wind and hail on a gravity wave in the Quad 
Cities area this morning, are ongoing in the vicinity of this 
surface low, while still nothing has formed further south 
along/ahead of the trailing front. SPC mesoanalysis suggests a 
narrow corridor of over 500 J/kg MLCAPE has developed along the 
front near/southeast of the St. Louis Metro, and with a few more 
hours of surface heating the RAP suggests this will increase 
further to around 1,000 J/kg over southwest Indiana/western 
Kentucky. In this unstable airmass, REFS expresses high (60-80%) 
confidence that storms will develop with forcing along the front, 
while a few additional showers may (30-40% chance) form on the nose 
of a developing LLJ across northern Kentucky/southern Indiana by 
around 5-6pm EST.

*** SEVERE WEATHER(?) THIS EVENING ***

Given the aforementioned instability and 30-40 kt deep layer shear, 
a few of these storms may become organized and produce localized 
severe weather upstream. However, by the time storms reach our neck 
of the woods, diurnally driven instability should be waning with the 
loss of surface heating (sunset is around 5:30 pm EST). In addition, 
the increase in shear number of showers and storms as the LLJ 
strengthens deeper into the evening will add abundant rain-cooled 
air to the environment - limiting the ability of any given cell to 
gain access to sufficient instability to become severe. Even so, if 
we should get any isolated cells with unobstructed storm relative 
inflow (from the southeast, per model hodographs), we could have 
localized severe wind and hail. Accordingly, SPC maintains a level 1 
of 5 (marginal) risk for both hazards across nearly our entire area 
with a recent upgrade to level 2 (slight) across our west, with the 
primary time window being between 6 and 9 pm EST.

*** BREEZY AND SHARPLY COOLER TONIGHT ***

The deepening surface low will pull a cold front across our area 
from the northwest tonight, ushering a cooler airmass into the 
region. While nocturnal timing will limit the depth of mixing, 3-
hour pressure rises of 3-4 mb behind the departing surface low will 
favor stiff winds out of the northwest - sustained around 15 mph 
with frequent gusts of 20+ (sporadically >25) mph. These winds will 
ease only slightly tomorrow morning as the surface pressure gradient 
weakens but mixing simultaneously deepens. REFS guidance is 
moderately confident (50-70% chance) that cloud cover sticks around 
for much of the day tomorrow given wrap around moisture, but below 
this stratocumulus layer steep low level lapse rates will favor some 
instability to fuel diurnal showers. This cloud cover and 
precipitation should confine temperatures to the upper 40s/low 50s 
throughout the day, but it will also limit cooling overnight into 
Friday morning - keeping our overnight lows in the mid 30s.

*** FIRST FLAKES OF THE SEASON ON FRIDAY? ***

Friday will be the coolest day of the forecast period with a 
reinforcing shot of cold air arriving from the north during the 
morning to bring 850mg temps down to -5 to -6 degC (per REFS mean). 
Forecast soundings suggest saturation may poke into the DGZ Friday 
morning across our east to result in a flake or two, but during the 
day temperatures should be just a little too warm - despite 
diurnally driven instability once again reaching the DGZ. With any 
lingering showers over the Bluegrass Friday evening (20% coverage), 
we may once again see a flake or two mix in, but the probability of 
anything sticking to pavement to cause impacts is very low.

*** EXTENDED FORECAST PERIOD ***

Winds should finally ease up Friday night, so with any breaks in 
cloud cover temperatures could take quite the dive. In fact, our 
forecast features lows in the mid 20s for many locations - locally 
low 20s in rural valleys. The upper level trough will linger long 
over the Great Lakes and Northeast, keeping the area seasonably cool 
(but dry) through early to mid next work week. However, long range 
models and their respective ensembles generally agree that by late 
week, upper level ridging will expand into the area from the west to 
favor a return to milder weather; NBM gives a 60-75% chance high 
temperatures return to the 60s by next Thursday (11/19).
